rule: Law 2003/003 article 9(1) requires a phytosanitary certificate for imports of plants and plant products; article 9(2) separately regulates when an import permit is needed. Decree 2005/0771 article 3 limits prior import permits to designated high-risk products; its article 8 specifically regulates origin certification for those high-risk goods but does not expressly waive the statutory certificate duty for other plant products. The later Joint Order of 4 March 2019, Annex I, expressly lists tea leaves and, separately, manufactured products within phytosanitary import/export inspection categories, includes parcel-carrier/courier platforms, and defines a shipment by coverage under one phytosanitary certificate. Treat the scoped identifiable dried sencha leaves as the listed tea-leaf commodity under article 9. This is an explicit scope inference: the tea-leaf entry does not itself say dried or steamed, and no Japan/sencha-specific ruling was found.
personalMailApplicability: The 2019 implementing inspection schedule expressly includes parcel carriers and couriers. No personal-use waiver of the article 9 certificate duty was established. The professional-importer registration requirements in the separate commercial e-Force permit workflow are not imposed here on the private recipient.
authority: Cameroon NPPO laws filed with IPPC
researchAttempts: Read product definitions and sections 3 and 9; examined implementing decree and searched processed-tea exemptions.

Read the 2023 MINADER compendium: Law 2003/003 pp143–144; Decree 2005/0771 pp154–155; Joint Order of 4 March 2019 pp173–177 including tea leaves, manufactured products and courier/post platforms. Searched the ministerial/NPPO high-risk commodity list and tea-specific determinations. Excluded an inspection fee listing as conclusive evidence of an import certificate requirement.

Final independent scope comparison: read Law 2003/003 articles 3 and 9 on printed pages 143–144 of the official 2023 MINADER compendium; Decree 2005/0771 articles 3 and 8 on pages 154–155; Joint Order 4 March 2019 Annex I on pages 176–177. Distinguished the statute's general certificate obligation from high-risk prior licensing. Reassessed the tea-leaf and manufactured-product listings together with the statutory duty, rather than treating an inspection fee alone as a requirement. The listing says tea leaves, not expressly dried/steamed tea; retained that inferential limit.

Read the GUCE announcement about the December 2024 MINADER permit digitization meeting and 2025 pilot. It describes the commercial operator application workflow but supplies no tea risk list or private-post exemption; it is not used as the basis for requiring a private recipient to register as a professional importer.
permitFreeReason: Exclude under the no-certificate constraint by applying the express tea-leaf inclusion in the 2019 phytosanitary schedule together with Law 2003/003 article 9(1), which requires certification of imported plant products. The fee schedule alone is not the legal basis for the certificate duty. Applying its tea-leaf item to steamed/dried retail sencha is a stated inference, not a published product ruling. This finding does not assert that an import permit is always required or that Japan-origin tea is designated high risk.
